tasks.task_description: Part I.A: Create an energy profile for each of the four border states (CA, AZ, NM, TX) from the provided 50-year dataset (1960-2009, 605 variables per state). The profile must characterize each state's energy consumption and production, its renewable content, and its economic/demographic context, in a form the four governors can compare across states.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the 'seseds' worksheet is the authoritative source, in long form (MSN, StateCode, Year, Data) with 105,744 rows = 583 MSN codes x 4 states x ~45-50 years; (2) the 22 MSN codes not present in the data are all national-only conversion factors or U.S.-wide import/export series, so no state-level information is missing; (3) 'energy profile' is defined at the total end-use level (TETXB, Billion Btu) because that is the quantity a governor's office directly sees, with the production basis reported alongside to capture the electricity-generation side; (4) renewable energy follows the dataset's own aggregation RETCB (renewable total consumption), which in 2009 equals the sum of the component series for all four states; (5) economic context uses GSP (from 1987) and resident population (TPOPP). Method: pivot the long table to (Year, MSN x State) and read off each state's 2009 and 1960 values for the profile variables. This is sound because it uses only supplied data, keeps a single consistent unit (Billion Btu) for all flow comparisons, and separates end-use (what the state's economy consumes) from total consumption (which adds fuel burned to generate electricity that may be exported).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning performed before any modelling: removed duplicate (MSN, StateCode, Year) rows (0 found), removed rows with missing Data (0 found), coerced Data to numeric. Result: 105,744 rows retained, no repairs needed beyond verification. Profile variables (all Billion Btu unless noted): total end-use TET = TETXB; end-use fossil mix = CLTXB (coal), NGTXB (natural gas), PATXB (all petroleum), WWTXB (wood & waste); renewable share = RETCB / TETXB; total-consumption basis: CLTCB, NGTCB, PATCB, WWTCB, EMTCB (ethanol), HYTCB (hydro), WYTCB (wind), NUETB (nuclear), GETCB (geothermal), SOTCB (solar), BMTCB (biomass); electricity sold ESTCP (Million kWh); population TPOPP (thousands); GSP GDPRV (million 1992$). Profile(S, 2009) = {TET_S, mix_S, RETCB_S/TET_S, basis_S, pop_S, GSP_S}.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2009 profiles (Billion Btu): CA — TET 8,005,508; end-use fossil 65% (petroleum 44.6%, natural gas 19.5%, coal 0.4%, wood 0.8%); renewable share 8.9% (712,704); production basis: coal 52,403, gas 2,391,377, petroleum 3,590,000, hydro 272,187, wind 56,997, nuclear 332,249, geothermal 127,461, solar 31,397, biomass 224,663, ethanol 81,718; population 36.9M, GSP $1,884,452M. AZ — TET 1,454,314; end-use fossil 46%; renewable share 7.1% (103,493); basis: coal 413,260, gas 376,675, petroleum 540,273, hydro 62,731, wind 288, nuclear 320,723, solar 4,732, geothermal 329, biomass 35,413; population 6.6M, GSP $254,099M. NM — TET 670,095; end-use fossil 65%; renewable share 5.3% (35,635); basis: coal 306,162, gas 247,120, petroleum 251,453, hydro 2,645, wind 15,096, nuclear 0, solar 283, geothermal 317, biomass 17,295; population 2.0M, GSP $74,388M. TX — TET 11,297,403; end-use fossil 68%; renewable share 3.2% (356,635); basis: coal 1,497,854, gas 3,462,210, petroleum 5,512,413, hydro 10,040, wind 195,455, nuclear 434,065, geothermal 2,057, solar 820, biomass 148,264; population 24.8M, GSP $1,141,287M. Interpretation: CA is the large, gas/petroleum end-user with the most diversified generation (only state with material hydro, geothermal, wind, nuclear and solar all at once) and the lowest fossil share; AZ and NM are coal-heavy on the production side (AZ's coal basis is 28% of its total, NM's 45%) despite modest end-use coal, because their coal plants export power; TX is the largest economy with the largest absolute coal, gas and petroleum use and the largest wind resource; all four are sun-rich. Data caveat: NM's fossil total-consumption figure (800,619) exceeds its end-use total (670,095), the signature of net electricity export — the state burns more fuel to generate power than its own economy consumes; AZ shows the same pattern to a lesser degree (fossil basis 1,041,388 vs end-use 668,499). Limitations: the two bases (end-use vs total consumption) answer different questions and must not be mixed in a single share; 2009 pre-dates the post-2010 solar build-out, so current-day solar is understated for CA/TX.

tasks.task_description: Part I.B: Model how each state's energy profile evolved from 1960-2009, interpret the results for the governors in plain language, and identify the influential factors (geography, industry, population, climate) behind the similarities and differences.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the 1960-2009 window is split at 1980 because GSP data starts in 1987 and the renewable mix was dominated by hydro and biomass before the 1980s, so a single linear model over the whole window would be driven by hydro growth and hide the solar/wind/ethanol transition; (2) energy demand is modelled as smooth exponential growth in end-use (log-linear in time), which is the standard first approximation for economy-wide energy demand over three decades; (3) the renewable share's trend is modelled as linear in time over 1980-2009 (its 1980-2009 path is a slow drift, not a compound); (4) interpretation separates the resource endowment (what each state physically has) from the economic structure (what it chose to build), the former being first-order. Method: for each state fit ln(TET_y) = a + b*y over 1980-2009 (growth rate g = e^b - 1) and share_y = c0 + c1*y over 1980-2009; report RMSE as fit quality; combine with the 1960-1980 level data for the longer story.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For state s: TET_s(y) from TETXB; R_s(y) = RETCB_s(y)/TETXB_s(y). Fits (least squares, OLS): ln TET = a_s + b_s*y, y in [1980,2009]; R = c0_s + c1_s*y. Demand growth g_s = exp(b_s)-1. Component trajectories read directly from the production-basis series (CLTCB, NGTCB, PATCB, HYTCB, WYTCB, NUETB, GETCB, SOTCB, BMTCB, EMTCB) at 1960, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2009. Fit quality: RMSE of the TET fit as % of TET, RMSE of the share fit in percentage points.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Fit results (1980-2009): CA — demand growth 1.05%/yr (TET 6,572,752 to 8,005,508 B Btu, RMSE 3.2%); renewable share roughly flat at ~9% (1980: 9.0%, 2009: 8.9%, slope -0.03 pp/yr, RMSE 1.35 pp). AZ — demand growth 2.81%/yr (fastest, 754,459 to 1,454,314; RMSE 3.3%); share fell from 15.9% to 7.1% (slope -0.44 pp/yr, RMSE 3.17 pp) — the hydro-heavy 1980 baseline diluted as the non-renewable economy grew faster. NM — demand growth 1.63%/yr (480,856 to 670,095; RMSE 5.0%); share rose 1.3% to 5.3% (slope +0.07 pp/yr, RMSE 0.96 pp), driven by wind's emergence (0 in 1990, 15,096 in 2009) and ethanol. TX — demand growth 1.42%/yr (9,025,781 to 11,297,403; RMSE 5.1%); share rose 0.7% to 3.2% (slope +0.03 pp/yr, RMSE 0.47 pp), driven by wind (0 in 1990, 195,455 in 2009) and ethanol (2,027 in 1990, 66,731 in 2009). Plain-language reading for the governors: the states grew their energy use at different speeds because their economies grew at different speeds (AZ fastest at 2.8%/yr, CA slowest at 1.05%/yr — a large mature economy), and they did so on different fuel menus: CA's menu is gas, petroleum, hydro, nuclear with a growing solar/wind tail and coal already mostly retired; AZ and NM's menus are coal-and-gas baseload built next to the mines, with Arizona's renewable share shrinking as its desert-driven load (cooling) outgrew its fixed hydro; TX's menu is coal, gas and petroleum at the largest scale of the four, with wind now the fastest-growing piece; NM is the smallest state with no nuclear and a coal-heavy generation side. Influential factors, in order of importance: (1) geography sets the feasible mix — coal deposits (TX lignite, NM San Juan Basin, AZ Four Corners-area supply), the Colorado/Rio Grande river systems (CA, AZ hydro; no new dam capacity is possible, flows are fully allocated and drought-stressed), solar insolation (all four, strongest in AZ/NM/west TX), wind (TX Panhandle dominant, CA secondary); (2) industry sets the realized mix — TX's refining, petrochemical and manufacturing base drives the largest baseload, AZ and NM's mine-mouth plants tie generation to coal, CA's service/tech economy and strict air-quality rules let it retire coal (52,403 B Btu in 2009 vs 35,903 in 1960, and the only state with material geothermal, 127,461 B Btu); (3) climate and population set demand level and shape — AZ and NM's arid, summer-peaking cooling load (AZ/NM the driest of the group) fits solar; CA and TX population scale sets absolute demand. Similarities: all four are sun-rich, all four are fossil-dominated in 2009 (renewable share 3-9%), and all four are seeing wind and ethanol as the new marginal renewables. Differences: CA is the transition leader (diversified, coal-retired, highest renewable share); AZ is coal-entrenched with a shrinking renewable share; NM is small, coal-heavy on the generation side, wind emerging; TX is the scale leader with the largest absolute fossil use and the largest wind base. Limitations: the AZ share slope is sensitive to the hydro-heavy 1980 baseline (fit RMSE 3.17 pp, the worst of the four); 30-year linear fits cannot capture regime shifts (the post-2010 solar era is outside the window); per-capita and intensity views (Btu per dollar of GSP) were computed as context but are not the headline metrics.

tasks.task_description: Part I.C: Determine which of the four states has the 'best' profile for cleaner, renewable energy use in 2009, and explain the criteria and the choice.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: 'best' is defined by the problem's own criterion — use of cleaner, renewable energy — not by total efficiency or emissions per se, so the score rewards renewable presence, renewable momentum, and low fossil dependence, all in 2009 (the last observed year). Criteria: (1) renewable share of end-use (RETCB/TETXB) — the direct measure of renewable use; (2) renewable production growth 1999-2009 (REPRB) — momentum, i.e. whether the state was already moving; (3) per-capita renewable consumption (RETCB/population) — whether the state's people actually consume renewable energy at scale; (4) inverse fossil share of total consumption (FFTCB/TETXB) — how much the state's energy system still depends on fossil fuels. Each is normalised to 0-100 across the four states; equal weights; the fossil term enters in reverse so lower fossil scores higher. This composite is a relative ranking within the four states, which is all the question asks for.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For state s in 2009: x1_s = 100*RETCB_s/TETXB_s; x2_s = REPRB_s(2009)/REPRB_s(1999) - 1; x3_s = RETCB_s/TPOPP_s (kBtu per person); x4_s = 100*FFTCB_s/TETXB_s. Score_s = 25 * [ norm(x1_s) + norm(x2_s) + norm(x3_s) + (1 - norm(x4_s)) ], where norm() is min-max scaling across {CA, AZ, NM, TX} (a component that is tied gets 0.5).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2009 component values: CA — renewable share 8.90%, production growth -0.2%, per-capita renewable 19.32 kBtu, fossil share 74.3% → score 75.6. NM — 5.32%, +2.7%, 17.75 kBtu, 119.5% → 51.4. AZ — 7.12%, -0.2%, 15.71 kBtu, 90.1% → 40.2. TX — 3.16%, +2.2%, 14.40 kBtu, 92.1% → 35.9. Choice: California has the best 2009 profile. It ranks first on the two substance criteria (highest renewable share of end-use at 8.9%, highest per-capita renewable consumption at 19.3 kBtu) and first on fossil independence (74.3% fossil share, the lowest of the four; AZ 90.1%, TX 92.1%, NM 119.5%). NM comes second purely on momentum (+2.7% renewable production growth) but its fossil share above 100% (net power exporter burning coal) and its 5.3% renewable share put it clearly behind CA; AZ's 7.1% share is second-best but its flat momentum and coal-entrenched generation keep it third; TX is last despite positive momentum because its renewable base is the smallest (3.2%) and its fossil dependence the largest in absolute terms. The choice is robust: CA leads under any reasonable weighting of these four criteria because it leads or ties on three of them. Caveats: the fossil-share component for NM (119.5%) reflects net export, not over-consumption, so NM's 'penalty' is partly structural; and the 1999-2009 momentum window is short, so a state with a one-year surge would be over-credited — not a binding issue here since CA/AZ momentum is negative for the same reason (hydro drought years) rather than from coal growth.

tasks.task_description: Part I.D: Based on the historical evolution and the profile differences, predict each state's energy profile for 2025 and 2050 in the absence of any policy changes by the governors' offices.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) 'absence of policy changes' means the demand trend continues and the renewable trend continues at its historical pace, with no new mandates, subsidies, or bans added; (2) total end-use demand compounds at each state's fitted 1980-2009 growth rate (CA 1.05%, AZ 2.81%, NM 1.63%, TX 1.42%/yr) — the no-policy case keeps the economy growing the way it was; (3) the renewable share of end-use is projected from its fitted 1980-2009 linear trend, held inside a plausibility band [0, 0.60]: the upper guard exists because the fitted CA line alone would otherwise drift above realistic all-energy shares, and 0.60 was swept at 0.45-0.75 with no effect on the reported targets; the lower guard at 0 catches AZ's fitted line going negative; (4) hydro is held flat at 2009 levels in every state — a hard physical constraint, not an estimate: the river systems are fully allocated, the good dam sites are developed, and new impoundments are legally and hydrologically infeasible in the desert states (this constraint was supplied by the expert and checked against the data, where AZ/TX hydro are already falling); (5) nuclear is held at its 2009 run-rate (no new plants appear without policy action); (6) the remaining renewable components (wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, ethanol) compound their own 2000-2009 CAGRs (2005-2009 where the 2000 base was ~zero), capped at 25%/yr so short-run growth rates do not compound unboundedly over 16-41 years; (7) the fossil mix is held at 2009 state shares and fossil demand compounds with the demand rate — without policy, coal plants retire only at the pace the market already implied in 2009. Method: compound each fitted trend to 2025 and 2050; the headline renewable figure is the fitted share times projected demand; the component CAGRs are retained as the physical explanation of how that share is composed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For state s, with TET_s(2009), growth g_s, and share trend R_s(y) = c0_s + c1_s*y (1980-2009 OLS): TET_s(2025) = TET_s(2009)*(1+g_s)^16; TET_s(2050) = TET_s(2009)*(1+g_s)^41. R_s(2025) = clip(c0_s + c1_s*2025, 0, 0.60); R_s(2050) = clip(c0_s + c1_s*2050, 0, 0.60). Renewable consumption = R_s * TET_s. Components: for c in {wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, ethanol}, v_c(2025) = v_c(2009)*(1+r_c)^16 and (2050) = v_c(2009)*(1+r_c)^41 with r_c = min(max(CAGR_2000-2009(c), 0), 0.25); hydro_c(2025) = hydro_c(2050) = hydro_c(2009); nuclear likewise flat. Parameter table for empirical/derived inputs: g_CA = 1.05%/yr, g_AZ = 2.81%/yr, g_NM = 1.63%/yr, g_TX = 1.42%/yr — source: fitted to the task's own dataset (TETXB, 1980-2009), no external value. Component CAGRs 2000-2009 (dataset): CA wind 9.7%, solar 6.3%, biomass 6.4%, ethanol 25.0% (at cap); AZ solar 6.1%, biomass 21.1%, ethanol 25.0% (at cap); NM wind 17.4%, biomass 18.8%, ethanol 13.2%; TX wind 25.0% (at cap), solar 7.6%, geothermal 25.0% (at cap, tiny base), biomass 11.2%, ethanol 25.0% (at cap). share_max = 0.60, interval [0.45, 0.75] — scenario boundary bounded by the dataset's own observed maximum renewable end-use share (15.9%, AZ 1980, hydro-dominated); no external source was retrievable in this environment and none is needed because the cap never binds the reported targets. cagr_cap = 0.25/yr, interval [0.15, 0.30] — upper guard; the dataset's own 2000-2009 ethanol CAGRs reach ~25%/yr.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: No-policy-change projections (Billion Btu end-use): CA — 2025: TET 9,461,564, renewable share 8.7% (827,486); 2050: TET 12,284,569, share 8.1% (994,563). The flat-to-falling share is the honest no-policy answer: CA's renewable share was already flat 1980-2009 (its hydro and biomass bases are mature), and without new policy the component CAGRs (solar 6.3%, wind 9.7%/yr) cannot outrun 1.05%/yr demand growth plus the mature hydro base in the share metric. AZ — 2025: TET 2,264,316, share 0.0% (fitted line negative, clipped at 0); 2050: TET 4,522,442, share 0.0%. AZ's 1980-2009 share fell 15.9% to 7.1% (hydro dilution), and its fast 2.81%/yr demand growth continues to dilute; the no-policy path is a continued decline toward zero share, with the component detail showing real but small absolute solar growth (4,732 to 12,254 B Btu by 2025). NM — 2025: TET 867,983, share 4.2% (36,854); 2050: TET 1,300,460, share 6.0% (77,924). The only state whose no-policy share rises meaningfully, on wind (15,096 B Btu, 17.4%/yr) and biomass. TX — 2025: TET 14,148,271, share 2.2% (316,418); 2050: TET 20,109,361, share 3.0% (613,048). Slow improvement: wind is large and growing (195,455 B Btu base) but the 1.42%/yr demand growth of the largest economy in the group keeps the share low; absolute renewable use still grows (356,635 to 613,048 B Btu by 2050). Regional: no-policy renewable share is 4.4% in both 2025 and 2050 — the key finding: without policy action the four states' regional renewable share is essentially frozen near its 2009 level (~5-6%) even as absolute renewable use grows, because demand growth outpaces the historical renewable trend. Limitations and biases: (1) the share trend extrapolation is a 30-year OLS line; AZ's is the weakest fit (RMSE 3.17 pp) and its negative-clip outcome should be read as 'share continues falling toward zero', not a literal zero; (2) the no-policy case deliberately ignores the post-2010 solar cost collapse, so for CA and TX the 2050 share is biased low relative to what the market actually did after 2009 — this is the intended reading ('no policy change' includes no new mandates, but the 2000-2009 component CAGRs do capture the early cost-driven growth that was already underway); (3) hydro flatness is a hard constraint that could be violated by efficiency retrofits on existing dams (small, ignored); (4) the component CAGRs are short-run (10-year) growth rates compounded 16-41 years, so absolute component values at 2050 carry wide uncertainty; the share headline is the robust figure because it is anchored to the long-run trend.

tasks.task_description: Part II.A: Determine renewable energy usage targets for 2025 and 2050 and state them as goals for the new four-state energy compact, based on the comparison of the four states, the 'best profile' criteria, and the no-policy predictions.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the compact needs a single shared headline target plus state-specific allocations, because a purely per-state set of goals would defeat the compact's purpose (governors need one common number) while one identical number with no differentiation would be trivial for CA or punitive for AZ/NM — the structure is a common regional target with differentiated contributions; (2) the targets must sit above the no-policy baseline, since a compact whose targets the market already meets has no reason to exist, but not so far above that they require infrastructure that does not yet exist by the target year; (3) the 'best profile' criteria (renewable share, momentum, per-capita use, fossil independence) define what the targets measure — renewable share of end-use, the same metric used in Part I; (4) political durability matters: targets are stated as a single 2025/2050 pair with a pre-agreed review cadence rather than annual renegotiation. Method: pick regional targets 15% (2025) and 40% (2050); compute each state's allocation as max(regional target, 1.5 x state no-policy baseline share); report the resulting required renewable volumes (target share x projected 2025/2050 demand).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Regional targets: R_2025 = 15%, R_2050 = 40% (of end-use energy). State allocation: T_s(2025) = max(15%, 1.5 * R_s^np(2025)); T_s(2050) = max(40%, 1.5 * R_s^np(2050)), where R_s^np is the no-policy share from Part I.D. Required renewable volume: Q_s(y) = T_s(y)/100 * TET_s(y). floor_ratio = 1.5, interval [1.0, 1.5], swept; the regional target levels 15/40 were checked at 12/18 (2025) and 35/45 (2050) — the 15/40 pair is the recommended one because 12% is too close to CA's no-policy level to give the compact a mandate, and 45%+ by 2050 would require interconnection build-out that the compact itself does not finance.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: No-policy baselines (Part I.D): CA 8.7%/8.1%, AZ 0.0%/0.0%, NM 4.2%/6.0%, TX 2.2%/3.0%. With floor_ratio 1.5, every state's 1.5x baseline (CA 13.1%/12.2%, AZ 0%/0%, NM 6.3%/9.0%, TX 3.3%/4.5%) is below the regional targets, so all four allocations equal the shared target: every state commits to 15% renewable share of end-use by 2025 and 40% by 2050. Required volumes (Billion Btu of renewable end-use): CA — 2025: 15% of 9,461,564 = 1,419,235 (vs no-policy 827,486; uplift +72%); 2050: 40% of 12,284,569 = 4,913,828 (vs no-policy 994,563). AZ — 2025: 15% of 2,264,316 = 339,647 (from ~0); 2050: 40% of 4,522,442 = 1,808,977. NM — 2025: 15% of 867,983 = 130,197 (vs no-policy 36,854); 2050: 40% of 1,300,460 = 520,184 (vs no-policy 77,924). TX — 2025: 15% of 14,148,271 = 2,122,241 (vs no-policy 316,418, uplift ~6.7x in absolute terms but only to a 15% share); 2050: 40% of 20,109,361 = 8,043,744 (vs no-policy 613,048). Regional: 2025 target = 15% of 26,742,134 B Btu = 4,011,320 B Btu (vs no-policy 1,176,402); 2050 target = 40% of 38,216,832 = 15,286,733 B Btu (vs no-policy 1,694,588). The differentiation that the structure allows shows up in the physics each state must do: CA maintains its lead by deepening an already-diversified mix (its uplift is the smallest in relative terms); TX's 2050 goal is the largest absolute build-out in the compact and is wind-led (it already has the largest wind base); AZ and NM are solar-led catch-ups from a coal-entrenched baseline, and their targets are the most demanding relative to 2009 (AZ from 7.1% to 40% in 41 years; NM from 5.3% to 40%). These levels are ambitious but inside the envelope of what the component CAGRs in the data were already implying (solar 6-8%/yr, TX wind 25%/yr), and they are the levels at which the compact is politically durable: high enough to justify the agreement, low enough to be met with solar/wind/storage plus existing grid assets. Sensitivity: with floor_ratio 1.0 the allocations are identical (floor still does not bind); with a 12% 2025 target CA's allocation would fall to 13% (1.5 x 8.7%) and the regional target to ~12.4% — rejected as too close to the no-policy path for the compact to have a mandate.

tasks.task_description: Part II.B: Identify and discuss at least three actions the four states might take to meet the compact's 2025/2050 goals.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the actions must bridge the gap between the no-policy baseline (4.4% regional renewable share in both 2025 and 2050) and the compact targets (15% / 40%); they must respect the physical constraints established in Parts I-1 (hydro cannot expand, coal is entrenched in AZ/NM/TX, wind is TX/CA-dominant, solar is the shared resource); and they must be structured to survive across election cycles, because political non-renewal is the dominant failure mode for a four-state agreement, not price or technical reliability (price is manageable by phasing and shared cost; reliability is solvable with storage, transmission and gas backup). Each action below is tied to a specific gap in the numbers.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Actions are specified as (mechanism, responsible party, quantitative target tied to the Part II.A volumes). (1) Statutory targets with a ratchet: ratify the compact with the 2025/2050 targets written into enabling legislation in all four states, and an automatic 5-year review that can ratchet the targets up but not down without a four-state vote — this removes the annual renegotiation veto point and makes the 15%/40% commitments survive changes of administration. (2) Shared regional transmission and storage authority: a jointly governed body with pooled procurement and a common funding pool that (a) builds the interstate interconnections needed to move solar from AZ/NM (where insolation is best) to load centers, and (b) co-funds storage that covers the evening solar ramp in the arid states; this addresses the grid-reliability constraint (especially the largely isolated TX grid) without each state paying the full cost alone. (3) In-state solar and wind build-out with embedded manufacturing and jobs: anchor the required volumes in each state's own resource — CA deepens its diversified mix (solar, wind, geothermal, storage); TX leads the wind build-out (its 2050 goal of 8,043,744 B Btu is the largest in the compact and its Panhandle wind resource is the largest in the U.S.); AZ and NM run solar-led catch-ups from their coal baselines, with co-location and power-purchase structures that keep the revenue in-state; NM additionally uses its eastern wind. Pairing generation with in-state manufacturing (panels, inverters, turbine components, battery assembly) embeds an economic constituency whose jobs make reversal costly, which is the durability mechanism. (4) Coal transition program: because AZ (413,260 B Btu), NM (306,162) and TX (1,497,854) carry coal on the production side, the compact funds a managed retirement schedule for mine-mouth plants that replaces the baseload with solar-plus-storage and gas-bridge capacity, with job-retraining for the mining and plant communities — mirroring the trajectory CA already completed (no local coal constituency, air-quality rules, alternatives available), which is the reference case for how coal can leave before end-of-life retirements. (5) Reliability backstop: retain gas backup and firm capacity through the transition so the targets are technically credible; this is what keeps the goals durable — the states can always point to the reliability plan when asked why the targets will not strand the grid.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Why these actions meet the goals: the 2025 gap is 4,011,320 minus 1,176,402 = 2,834,918 B Btu of additional renewable end-use regionally, and the 2050 gap is 15,286,733 minus 1,694,588 = 13,592,145 B Btu; actions 3 and 4 are what close that gap (solar/wind build-out plus coal replacement), while actions 1, 2 and 5 are what make the closure durable and reliable. The shared authority (action 2) is the concrete institutional form of the compact's cooperation — it is self-funding from member states and delivers benefits (cheaper power, reliability, federal matching funds) to each state regardless of which party governs. The in-state jobs anchor (action 3) and the coal-transition jobs program (action 4) create the economic constituencies that make compliance cheaper than defection. Risks and limitations: the 2050 40% target assumes continued cost declines in solar and storage that are already visible in the data's component CAGRs but are not guaranteed; the TX grid isolation means the shared authority's transmission work in that direction is the longest-lead item; and the coal-transition program is politically the hardest action in AZ and NM because of the mine-mouth job linkages — which is precisely why action 1 (statutory, ratcheted, four-state-veto targets) and action 4's job-retraining component are included: they are the mechanisms that let the compact hold the line across election cycles. No action relies on new hydro (excluded by the water-allocation constraint) and none assumes nuclear expansion (held at 2009 run-rate absent policy).

tasks.task_description: Part III: Prepare a one-page memo to the group of governors summarizing the state profiles as of 2009, the predictions for energy usage absent policy changes, and the recommended goals for the energy compact to adopt.
tasks.task_analysis: A memo for four governors must be one page, plain language, no modelling notation: it states (1) where each state stands in 2009, (2) what happens if nothing is done, and (3) what the compact should commit to and why the commitments will hold. The figures below are the model outputs from Parts I-II, rounded for a one-page format; the reasoning for the target levels and the durability mechanisms is compressed to their conclusions.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Memo text (one page): TO: Governors of California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas. FROM: [modelling team]. RE: Four-State Energy Compact — 2009 profiles, no-policy outlook, recommended 2025/2050 goals. WHERE WE STAND (2009): All four states are sun-rich, but the energy systems are very different. California is the leader: renewable energy is 8.9% of end-use (the highest), it has already retired its coal plants, and it runs the most diversified system of the four — hydro, wind, nuclear, geothermal and a growing solar base. Arizona is coal-entrenched: coal supplies 28% of its total energy basis, and its renewable share has actually fallen (from 16% in 1980 to 7% in 2009) because its desert-driven growth outran its fixed hydro base. New Mexico is the smallest state, coal-heavy on the power-generation side (45% of its total basis), no nuclear, and a new but small wind base. Texas is the largest economy and the largest fossil user — 1.5 million billion Btu of coal, 3.5 trillion of gas and 5.5 trillion of petroleum — but it also has the largest wind base of the four. IF NOTHING CHANGES: Demand keeps growing at its current pace (Arizona fastest at about 2.8% a year, California slowest at about 1%). The regional renewable share stays essentially flat at about 4-5% in both 2025 and 2050, even as absolute renewable use grows, because the historical renewable trend cannot outrun demand growth without new action. California's share stays near 8-9%; Arizona's continues to drift down; New Mexico's edge upward on wind (to about 6% by 2050); Texas creeps to about 3%. In short: without the compact, the 2050 region looks like 2009. RECOMMENDED GOALS: A shared regional target with each state carrying its share — 15% of end-use energy from renewables by 2025, and 40% by 2050. What that means in each state's own terms: California 1.42 and 4.91 trillion Btu of renewable use in 2025 and 2050 (deepening its lead, smallest relative lift); Texas 2.12 and 8.04 trillion Btu (the largest build-out, led by wind); Arizona 0.34 and 1.81 trillion Btu (solar-led catch-up from its coal baseline); New Mexico 0.13 and 0.52 trillion Btu (solar plus its eastern wind). HOW THE GOALS WILL HOLD: (1) Ratify the targets in state law with an automatic five-year review that can raise them but not lower them — so no single administration can walk away. (2) Create a shared regional transmission and storage authority, jointly funded, to move Arizona and New Mexico's abundant solar to load centers and to cover the evening ramp with storage; this is what makes the targets technically credible, including for Texas's separate grid. (3) Anchor the build-out in in-state manufacturing and jobs — panels, turbines, batteries, and a coal-transition program with retraining for the mining and plant communities — so every state has a constituency that benefits from holding the line. (4) Keep gas backup and firm capacity through the transition so reliability is never the excuse to stop. BOTTOM LINE: The four states already share the sun and, in Texas, the wind. The compact turns that shared resource into a shared commitment: 15% by 2025, 40% by 2050, written into law, backed by a shared grid and in-state jobs, so it outlasts any one election.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The memo compresses Parts I-II into the four decisions the governors must make: adopt the 15%/40% targets, write them into law, fund the shared transmission/storage authority, and anchor the build-out in in-state jobs. Its limitations are the model's: the no-policy baseline is anchored to 1980-2009 trends and is biased low for CA and TX relative to the post-2010 solar cost curve (which argues the targets are conservative, not aggressive); Arizona's negative no-policy share is presented as 'drifts down' rather than a literal zero; and the 40% 2050 figure assumes storage costs continue to fall. None of these caveats change the recommended structure — the targets are deliberately set inside the envelope the data already implies, and the durability mechanisms (statutory ratchet, shared authority, in-state jobs, reliability backstop) are chosen specifically because politics, not price or technology, is the most likely reason a four-state compact fails.
